lesson.title: Why CMRR Matters: Rejecting the Noise You Didn't Ask For
lesson.summary: Common-mode rejection is the practical payoff of a high CMRR: it is what lets a differential circuit recover a clean signal in a noisy real-world environment by canceling interference that lands equally on both input wires.
lesson.body:
Real-world common-mode interference comes from predictable places: mains hum at 50 or 60Hz picked up by long cable runs, ground potential differences between two pieces of equipment, and radiated electromagnetic interference from nearby machinery or wiring. These sources tend to couple onto both conductors of a twisted pair or shielded cable almost equally, since the two wires run right next to each other and pick up essentially the same interference along their length. The wanted signal, meanwhile, exists specifically as the difference between the two wires. This is exactly why sensors are wired differentially in the first place: whatever noise the cable accumulates along its run looks like a common-mode signal to the amplifier at the far end, not a differential one, and a high-CMRR amplifier can reject it.

A finite CMRR means a common-mode voltage Vcm at the input produces a small unwanted contribution at the output equal to Acm times Vcm, where Acm = Ad divided by the CMRR ratio (not the dB value, the plain ratio it represents).

Bring back the instrumentation amplifier from earlier, with Ad = 11 and a desired output of 110mV from a 10mV differential input, and now assume a CMRR of 80dB, a realistic figure for an instrumentation-amplifier-grade circuit. Converting from dB to a ratio: CMRR ratio = 10 to the power of (80/20) = 10 to the 4th power = 10,000. So Acm = Ad / CMRR ratio = 11 / 10,000 = 0.0011. Suppose the sensor cable also picks up 1V of common-mode 60Hz hum, appearing equally on both leads (Vcm = 1V). That contributes an output error of Acm times Vcm = 0.0011 times 1V = 0.0011V, or 1.1mV. Compared with the desired 110mV output, that hum error is 1.1 / 110, which works out to 0.01, or about 1 percent of the reading, small in this case but not zero.

Two levers control that final error, and neither substitutes for the other: reducing Vcm itself through shielded or twisted-pair cabling and careful grounding practice, and raising CMRR by choosing an instrumentation amplifier over a plain resistor-based difference amplifier and keeping resistors well matched. A cleaner cable and a better amplifier both shrink the same error term from different sides.
